# Multiple sclerosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Neuromuscular disorders > Multiple sclerosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/WR0PNf)

---

## Summary

Multiple <u>sclerosis</u> (MS) is a chronic degenerative disease of the <u>CNS</u> characterized by <u>demyelination</u> and axonal degeneration in the <u>brain</u> and spinal cord, which are caused by an immune-mediated inflammatory process. The <u>prevalence</u> of MS is higher among women and people in temperate regions such as Europe and North America. Impaired <u>vision</u> (due to <u>retrobulbar neuritis</u>) is usually the first manifestation of MS; other neurological deficits appear as the disease progresses. The most common clinical course is characterized by exacerbations followed by periods of complete or incomplete remission. Diagnosis is made using clinical and <u>MRI</u> findings to identify the dissemination of <u>CNS</u> lesions in time and space. Characteristic <u>MRI</u> findings are <u>demyelinated</u> <u>sclerotic</u> <u>plaques</u> primarily located in <u>white matter</u>. Differential diagnoses of MS include other chronic <u>demyelinating</u> diseases and neurological infections (e.g., <u>borreliosis</u>, <u>neurosyphilis</u>). Acute exacerbations of MS are usually treated with high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>. Between exacerbations, patients may be treated with disease-modifying drugs (e.g., <u>interferon beta</u>, <u>glatiramer acetate</u>, <u>natalizumab</u>). There is currently no definitive treatment for MS.

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (3:1) [[1]](/library/S4Xyiy)

* Age of onset: : 20–40 years of age [[2]](/library/OfbImG)

* Ethnicity: ↑ <u>prevalence</u> among the white and black population [[3]](/library/R81lmi0)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 50-300 per 100 000 people (greater among people who live farther from the equator)  [[2]](/library/OfbImG)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The etiology of multiple <u>sclerosis</u> is unclear; it is believed to develop in genetically predisposed people who have been exposed to certain environmental factors.




* Genetic predisposition

* Presence of <u>HLA</u>-DRB1*15 <u>allele</u> increases the risk of MS. [[4]](/library/DiY1FK)

* Presence of <u>HLA</u>-A*02 <u>allele</u> appears to be protective against MS. [[4]](/library/DiY1FK)

* 35% disease <u>concordance</u> among <u>monozygotic twins</u> [[5]](/library/h4XcQy)

* 3–4% disease <u>concordance</u> among first-degree relatives [[5]](/library/h4XcQy)

* Environmental <u>risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/OfbImG)[[6]](/library/wiYhFK)

* Low <u>vitamin D</u> levels (insufficient intake, decreased exposure to UV radiation)

* <u>Cigarette smoking</u>

* Pathogens: <u>EBV</u>, <u>HHV 6</u>

* <u>Obesity</u> early in life

---

## Classification

### Definitions [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[8]](/library/qU1CVT0)




* MS exacerbation

* New symptoms or significant worsening of symptoms caused by <u>CNS</u> <u>demyelination</u> that last at least 24 hours and are not accompanied by <u>fever</u> or infection

* Also referred to as an attack, relapse, or flare

* Remission: a period of recovery after an exacerbation during which clinical symptoms resolve completely or almost completely

* Pseudorelapse: recurrence or significant worsening of existing symptoms due to stressors (e.g., infection, heat)

* Radiologically isolated syndrome (<u>RIS</u>) [[9]](/library/akXQmy)

* The presence of <u>demyelinating</u> lesions characteristic of MS in an asymptomatic individual

* Not considered an MS <u>phenotype</u> but may progress to MS

* Clinically isolated syndrome (CIS)

* A single episode of neurological symptoms resulting from <u>CNS</u> <u>demyelination</u>

* A second episode of such symptoms increases the likelihood that the symptoms are not clinically isolated and that the patient meets the diagnostic criteria for MS.

* <u>Diffuse cerebral sclerosis</u> (Schilder disease) [[10]](/library/FU1gUT0)[[11]](/library/8U1OUT0)

* A rare inflammatory <u>demyelinating</u> <u>CNS</u> condition that affects children and young adults

* Large areas of <u>demyelination</u> lead to various neurological deficits and psychological changes.





### Clinical course [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[12]](/library/_4X5Ny)[[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)




| <br>Clinical phenotypes of multiple sclerosis [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[12]](/library/_4X5Ny)[[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Phenotype</u> | Characteristics | Frequency |
| Relapsing-remitting MS (<u>RR-MS</u>) | <br><br>* Exacerbations occur.<br><br>* Symptoms remit almost completely between exacerbations.<br><br><br> | <br>* ∼ 90% (most common clinical course)<br><br> |
| Secondary progressive MS(<u>SP-MS</u>) | <br>* A progression of <u>RR-MS</u> characterized by continuous worsening of neurological function that occurs independently of exacerbation events<br><br> | <br>* ∼ 50% of patients with <u>RR-MS</u> develop <u>SP-MS</u>.<br><br> |
| Primary progressive MS (<u>PP-MS</u>) | <br>* Symptoms continuously worsen from the onset of the disease.<br><br> | <br>* ∼ 10%<br><br> |

## Pathophysiology

* Pathophysiology of MS is characterized by autoimmune inflammation, <u>demyelination</u>, and axonal degeneration.

* Most commonly accepted theory: Activation of autoreactive <u>T-lymphocytes</u>;   → inflammatory processes → focal <u>demyelination</u> with partial preservation of <u>axons</u> (acute <u>plaques</u>) → loss of <u>axons</u> and <u>atrophy</u> of <u>oligodendrocytes</u> (chronic <u>plaques</u>) → <u>gliosis</u>  → inadequate remyelination

* <u>B-lymphocyte</u> dysfunction: The following suggests that <u>B-lymphocytes</u> play a role in the pathogenesis of MS, although the exact mechanism of their involvement is unclear.

* Anti-<u>CD20</u> agents (<u>ocrelizumab</u>, <u>ofatumumab</u>, <u>rituximab</u>) are effective in preventing exacerbations.

* Presence of tertiary lymphoid organs in the <u>meninges</u> of individuals with <u>secondary progressive MS</u>  [[14]](/library/R4XlQy)

* Intrathecal synthesis of <u>IgG</u> (<u>oligoclonal bands</u>; see “Diagnostics” section for more information)

* Progressive <u>phenotypes</u> (forms) of MS are characterized by [[15]](/library/u4XpOy)

* <u>Chronic inflammation</u> that occurs with an intact <u>blood-brain barrier</u> and is driven by <u>immune cells</u> compartmentalized in the <u>leptomeninges</u> and perivascular spaces

* Accelerated compared to relapsing-remitting <u>phenotype</u> <u>brain atrophy</u>

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>: fatigue, <u>headache</u>

* <u>Optic neuritis</u> ;  [[16]](/library/mvaV05)[[17]](/library/5vai05)[[18]](/library/KvaUa5)

* Most often the earliest manifestation

* Typically unilateral

* Can be painful

* Impaired <u>vision</u> and <u>color blindness</u>

* <u>Relative afferent pupillary defect</u> (<u>Marcus Gunn pupil</u>)

* <u>Internuclear ophthalmoplegia</u> (<u>INO</u>) as a result of a lesion in the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> (<u>MLF</u>) 

* <u>Ipsilateral</u> <u>medial rectus</u> <u>weakness</u> but an intact <u>convergence</u> reflex

* Disconjugate, <u>lateral</u> gaze <u>nystagmus</u> in the <u>contralateral</u> <u>eye</u>

* More frequently bilateral than unilateral

* <u>Demyelination</u> of <u>spinal cord tracts</u>

* Lhermitte sign: a shooting electric sensation that travels down the <u>spine</u> upon <u>flexion</u> of the neck

* <u>Pyramidal tract</u> lesion: <u>upper motor neuron</u> <u>weakness</u>, <u>spasticity</u>, <u>hyperreflexia</u>, positive <u>Babinski sign</u>, impaired gait

* <u>Dorsal</u> spinal column lesion: loss of vibration and fine-touch sensation, numbness, <u>paresthesias</u>, <u>sensory ataxia</u> usually involving the trunk or one or more limbs

* <u>Neuropathic pain</u> (see “<u>Central neuropathic pain</u>”)

* Absent <u>abdominal reflex</u>  [[19]](/library/nva705)

* <u>Cerebellar</u> involvement: poor postural control, imbalance, gait dysfunction, Charcot neurological triad:  of <u>scanning speech</u>, <u>nystagmus</u>, and <u>intention tremors</u>

* <u>Transverse myelitis</u>

* Asymmetric <u>paraplegia</u>, unilateral sensory loss, <u>bladder</u> dysfunction

* Partial <u>transverse myelitis</u> is a common early manifestation of MS, causing asymmetric neurologic dysfunction below the lesion.

* <u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>: <u>diplopia</u>, <u>facial palsy</u>, <u>trigeminal neuralgia</u> (can be bilateral) ;  [[20]](/library/wdWhH40)[[21]](/library/4fW3mk0)

* <u>Trigeminal neuralgia</u> (TN) typically manifests unilaterally.

* Bilateral TN should raise concern for MS, especially in younger patients.

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>: bowel and <u>bladder</u> neurogenic disorders (e.g., <u>urinary incontinence</u>), impaired sexual function

* Changes in mental state: <u>depression</u>, emotional changes, <u>memory</u> deficits, impaired concentration

* Uhthoff phenomenon: a reversible exacerbation of neurological symptoms following an increase in body temperature, e.g., physical exertion, a warm bath, or <u>fever</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Fundoscopy</u> is normal in 60% of cases of <u>optic neuritis</u>. Neither the patient nor the doctor are able to see anything.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Uhthoff phenomenon</u> triggered by a viral infection may mimic an exacerbation of MS.




> [!TIP]
> MS is a chronic condition that typically manifests in a relapsing-remitting form characterized by episodic <u>CNS</u> dysfunction (exacerbations) with at least partial recovery between episodes.

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[22]](/library/WDYPWr)




* Diagnosis of MS depends on a combination of clinical findings (e.g., <u>optic neuritis</u>, <u>Lhermitte sign</u>, sensory abnormalities, <u>cerebellar signs</u>), imaging, and laboratory results.

* Consider early specialist (i.e., <u>neurology</u>) consultation for patients with history and clinical features suggestive of MS.

* The McDonald Criteria for both DIT and DIS must both be met to confirm a diagnosis of MS: [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)

* <u>Dissemination in time</u> (DIT): the appearance of new <u>CNS</u> lesions over time that can be confirmed clinically, with imaging, or with <u>CSF analysis</u>

* <u>Dissemination in space</u> (DIS): the presence of lesions in different regions of the <u>CNS</u> that can be confirmed clinically or in <u>MRI</u>

* In some cases, electrophysiological, <u>CSF</u>, and <u>laboratory studies</u> may be necessary to support the diagnosis and exclude differential diagnoses.  [[23]](/library/CGcqYV0)





![McDonald Criteria for diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis](media/fa2dgh8fexdg9hietq8yscf8.jpg)

McDonald Criteria for diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis




> [!TIP]
> Clinical evidence or <u>MRI</u> findings consistent with the presence of <u>CNS</u> lesions that are disseminated in both time and space confirm the diagnosis of MS.




### Imaging for MS [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)




<u>MRI</u> is the imaging study of choice for the diagnosis and monitoring of MS.




* Indications

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> (with and without <u>gadolinium</u>): all patients with suspected MS

* <u>MRI</u> spinal cord (with and without <u>gadolinium</u>): to increase diagnostic yield (e.g., in patients with nondiagnostic <u>brain</u> <u>MRI</u> or symptoms of partial <u>myelitis</u> ) [[24]](/library/vGcAaV0)

* Typical findings on <u>MRI</u>

* Multiple <u>sclerotic</u> <u>plaques</u> (most commonly found in the periventricular <u>white matter</u>) ; with finger-like radial extensions (Dawson fingers) related to <u>demyelination</u> and <u>reactive gliosis</u>  [[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)[[23]](/library/CGcqYV0)

* In T1: <u>hypointense</u> or <u>isointense</u> lesions (i.e., black hole lesions) due to severe <u>demyelination</u> and axonal destruction  [[25]](/library/wGchYV0)

* In T2 and <u>FLAIR</u>: <u>hyperintense</u> lesions, typically round or oval in shape and found in both hemispheres [[26]](/library/xGcEYV0)

* Contrast-<u>enhancement</u> of active lesions; usually resolves after 2–8 weeks [[26]](/library/xGcEYV0)

### Additional studies




Consider further testing for patients with nondiagnostic <u>MRI</u> and to rule out differential diagnoses.




* <u>CSF</u> examination: commonly performed to support MS diagnosis and rule out other conditions [[1]](/library/S4Xyiy)[[27]](/library/ctcacV0)[[28]](/library/xW1Enf0)

* Oligoclonal bands [[23]](/library/CGcqYV0)

* <u>Oligoclonal bands</u> in the <u>CSF</u> but not in blood support diagnosis of MS.

* <u>Oligoclonal bands</u> manifest due to increased production of multiple nonspecific <u>IgG</u> sub-fractions in the <u>CSF</u>, which are caused by intrathecal inflammation.

* Detected using <u>electrophoresis</u> or <u>isoelectric focusing</u> of <u>CSF</u>

* Other common findings: moderate <u>lymphocytic</u> <u>pleocytosis</u>, increased <u>myelin</u> basic protein   [[28]](/library/xW1Enf0)

* <u>Evoked potentials</u>: Consider <u>visual evoked potentials</u> for patients with symptoms related to <u>vision</u>.  [[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)

* Can provide objective evidence of lesions

* May show evidence of increased latency, which occurs due to slowed <u>optic nerve</u> conduction.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: to rule out other diagnoses, based on clinical suspicion [[13]](/library/9GcNYV0)

* Commonly ordered: <u>CBC</u>, <u>vitamin B12</u>, <u>TSH</u>, <u>ESR</u>, <u>ANA</u>, <u>RPR</u>, <u>serologic testing</u> for <u>Lyme disease</u>

* Others: specific <u>autoantibodies</u> (e.g., <u>antiphospholipid antibodies</u>, <u>anti-SSA</u>, <u>anti-SSB</u>), <u>HIV testing</u>

* <u>Physical examination</u>: downwards pronator drift in <u>pronator drift test</u>

* An examination finding of asymmetric <u>pronation</u> and drifting movement of the arms when the patient stands with outstretched arms and closed eyes

* <u>Cerebellar</u> lesions typically cause <u>pronation</u> and upwards drift; <u>upper motor neuron lesions</u> typically cause <u>pronation</u> and downwards drift.





> [!TIP]
> The presence of multiple <u>oligoclonal bands</u> in <u>CSF</u> and their absence in the blood is highly suggestive of MS.  [[27]](/library/ctcacV0)[[29]](/library/1tc2cV0)

## Differential diagnoses

### Autoimmune diseases associated with inflammatory <u>demyelination</u>




#### Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (<u>NMOSD</u>; previously known as Devic disease or <u>neuromyelitis optica</u>) [[30]](/library/sxbtBD)[[31]](/library/txbXyD)




* Definition: immune-mediated, chronic inflammatory disorders of the <u>CNS</u> that primarily affect the <u>optic nerve</u> and spinal cord

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Incidence</u>: 0.3-4.4 per 100,000

* More prevalent in individuals of African and Asian descent than in white populations

* Peak onset: 40-60 years

* Pathophysiology

* Not fully understood but is thought to be an autoimmune process

* Anti-aquaporin-4 (an <u>autoantibody</u> that targets <u>aquaporin</u>-4 in the membrane of <u>astrocytes</u>) is involved in a <u>humoral immune response</u>

* Process characterized by <u>demyelination</u> and axonal damage of the <u>optic nerve</u> and spinal cord

* Clinical features

* Closely resembles the clinical appearance of MS

* Recurrent acute attacks with rapid stepwise deterioration, but no progression in between the attacks 

* <u>Optic neuritis</u> (often bilateral): impaired <u>vision</u>, retrobulbar <u>pain</u>

* <u>Transverse myelitis</u>: symmetric <u>paraplegia</u>, sensory loss, <u>bladder</u> dysfunction

* Diagnosis: based on

* Serological evidence of <u>anti-aquaporin-4</u> (<u>AQP4</u>)

* The presence of clinical characteristics

* <u>Optic neuritis</u>

* Acute <u>myelitis</u>

* <u>Area postrema</u> syndrome (episodes of intractable <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, and/or <u>hiccups</u>)

* Acute <u>brainstem syndrome</u>

* <u>Narcolepsy</u> or acute <u>diencephalic</u> syndrome with typical <u>MRI</u> lesions

* Cerebral syndrome with typical <u>brain lesions</u>

* Typical <u>MRI</u> findings (see clinical criteria for <u>NMOSD</u> with negative <u>AQP4</u>-<u>IgG</u> or unknown status below)





| Diagnostic criteria of <u>NMOSD</u> based on <u>AQP4</u>-<u>IgG</u> status |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serological criteria | Clinical criteria | Additional criteria |
| <br>Positive <u>AQP4</u>-<u>IgG</u> <br> | <br>* Presence of ≥ 1 clinical characteristic<br><br>* <u>Optic neuritis</u><br><br>* Acute <u>myelitis</u><br><br>* <u>Area postrema</u> syndrome<br><br>* Acute <u>brainstem syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Narcolepsy</u> or acute <u>diencephalic</u> syndrome with typical <u>MRI</u> lesions<br><br>* Cerebral syndrome with typical <u>brain lesions</u><br><br> | <br>* Exclusion of other causes (e.g., MS)<br><br> |
| Negative <u>AQP4</u>-<u>IgG</u> or unknown status | <br>* Presence of ≥ 2 clinical characteristics (see above)<br><br>* <u>Optic neuritis</u>, acute <u>myelitis</u>, or <u>area postrema</u> syndrome must be present.<br><br>* <u>Dissemination in space</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u> findings (see additional criteria)<br><br> | <br><br>* Exclusion of other causes (e.g., MS)<br><br>* <u>MRI</u> findings<br><br>* Acute <u>optic neuritis</u>: normal <u>cranial</u> <u>MRI</u> findings, nonspecific lesions in the <u>white matter</u>, a T2-<u>hyperintense</u> lesion, or a T1-<u>gadolinium</u> enhancing lesion of the <u>optic nerve</u> involving > 50% of the <u>optic nerve</u> or the <u>optic chiasma</u><br><br>* <u>Acute transverse myelitis</u>: longitudinal <u>spinal cord lesions</u> that extend ≥ 3 segments<br><br>* <u>Area postrema</u> syndrome: lesions in the <u>dorsal</u> medulla or <u>area postrema</u><br><br>* Acute <u>brainstem syndrome</u>: periependymal <u>brainstem</u> lesions<br><br><br> |




* Treatment

* First line: high-dose <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy for 3–5 days followed by a taper for 2–8 weeks

* <u>Plasmapheresis</u> in severe, refractory cases

* The following <u>biological agents</u> are approved for use in patients with positive <u>AQP4</u>-<u>IgG</u>

* <u>Eculizumab</u>: <u>antibody</u> against C5 <u>complement component</u>

* Inebilizumab: <u>antibody</u> against <u>CD19</u>

* Satralizumab: <u>antibody</u> against <u>IL-6</u> <u>receptor</u>

* Immune modulators used <u>off-label</u> (<u>azathioprine</u>, <u>rituximab</u>) may also reduce the risk of acute attacks

* <u>Natalizumab</u> and IFN-β (effective MS treatment options) can trigger <u>NMOSD</u> exacerbations




#### <u>Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis</u> (ADEM, <u>acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis</u>) [[32]](/library/KjaUYk)




* Definition: an immune-mediated, <u>demyelinating</u> <u>CNS</u> disease of parainfectious origin (e.g., <u>measles</u>) or after <u>vaccinations</u> (less common)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: mostly affects children and young adults

* Clinical features: rapidly progressing, usually monophasic, course with multifocal symptoms 

* Evidence of motor, sensory, <u>cranial nerve</u>, and/or <u>brainstem</u> impairment

* <u>Altered mental status</u> (<u>loss of consciousness</u> is possible)

* <u>Optic neuritis</u>: impaired <u>vision</u>, retrobulbar <u>pain</u>

* Diagnosis

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u>: <u>lymphocytic</u> <u>pleocytosis</u> and elevated protein

* Spinal and/or <u>brain</u> <u>MRI</u> (with and without contrast): typically multiple, bilateral lesions

* Treatment

* High-dose IV <u>corticosteroid</u> therapy for 3–5 days

* IV <u>immune globulin</u> therapy or plasma exchange in patients who do not respond to <u>corticosteroids</u>

* <u>Acyclovir</u> (empiric therapy until infectious etiology is identified)





### Other conditions




#### Transverse myelitis [[33]](/library/UPcbVc0)




* Definition: an acute or subacute inflammatory <u>myelopathy</u> that results in motor, sensory, and autonomic symptoms below the level of the affected segment

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Rare condition (< 5 cases per million)

* Bimodal <u>incidence</u>: peak in the 2<sup>nd</sup> and 4<sup>th</sup> decade of life

* Etiology

* Most often <u>idiopathic</u>

* Parainfectious (e.g., <u>enteroviruses</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>CMV</u>, <u>Listeria monocytogenes</u>, <u>B. burgdorferi</u>)

* <u>CNS</u> <u>demyelinating</u> disorders (e.g., multiple <u>sclerosis</u>, <u>neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders</u>)

* Systemic inflammatory autoimmune disorders (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>)

* <u>Paraneoplastic syndromes</u>

* Drug-induced (e.g., <u>TNF-α inhibitors</u>, <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u>)

* Clinical features

* Course of the disease

* Acute or subacute onset: symptoms may reach their peak between 4 hours and 21 days after onset

* Acute <u>spinal shock</u> may be present at onset

* Later, <u>spasticity</u>, <u>hyperreflexia</u>, and signs of <u>upper motor neuron</u> involvement (e.g., positive <u>Babinski sign</u>) may develop

* Neurologic dysfunction 

* Motor dysfunction (e.g., <u>paresis</u>, <u>paraplegia</u>)

* Sensory dysfunction (e.g., numbness, <u>paresthesias</u>, circumferential <u>dysesthesia</u> directly above the <u>sensory level</u>)

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>bladder</u> and/or <u>bowel incontinence</u>, <u>sexual dysfunction</u>)





| Overview of <u>transverse myelitis</u> types |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Types of TM |  | Manifestations | <u>MRI</u> findings |
| <br>Longitudinally limited TM (LLTM) | <br>Acute complete TM (ACTM) | <br>* Bilateral <u>paresis</u>, sensory dysfunction, and <u>autonomic dysfunction</u> below the level of the affected segment<br><br> | <br>* A single lesion spanning 1–2 <u>vertebral</u> segments and involves the full width of the spinal cord or the entire central part of the spinal cord<br><br> |
| <br>Acute partial TM (APTM)1 | <br>* Asymmetric neurologic dysfunction that can be attributed to injury of a specific <u>spinal tract</u>; may manifest as:<br><br>* <u>Brown-Séquard syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Central cord syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior cord syndrome</u><br><br> | <br>* A single lesion spanning 1–2 <u>vertebral</u> segments that involves individual sections (i.e., <u>spinal tracts</u>) of the spinal cord<br><br> |  |
| <br>Longitudinally extensive TM (LETM) |  | <br>* Either <u>incomplete spinal cord dysfunction</u> or <u>complete spinal cord dysfunction</u><br><br> | <br>* A lesion that extends over ≥ 3 <u>vertebral</u> segments; usually affects > 60% of the spinal cord thickness with involvement of the central spinal cord<br><br> |





* Diagnostics

* <u>MRI</u> of the <u>brain</u> and <u>spine</u> with and without <u>gadolinium</u>: investigation of choice 

* Finding: focal, <u>gadolinium</u>-enhancing lesion in the spinal cord (<u>T2-weighted</u> sequence)

* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u> with and without <u>gadolinium</u> should also be performed to rule out <u>CNS</u> <u>demyelinating</u> disorders (e.g., MS)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>Serological testing</u> for viral infections, <u>syphilis</u>, and <u>HIV</u> <u>antibodies</u>

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u> (<u>ESR</u>, <u>CRP</u>)

* Serum autoimmune <u>antibody</u> testing: <u>antinuclear antibodies</u>, <u>rheumatoid factor</u>, <u>antiphospholipid antibodies</u>, <u>NMO</u> <u>IgG</u> (<u>anti-aquaporin-4</u>)

* Serum levels of <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> and <u>methylmalonic acid</u>

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>CSF analysis</u> [[34]](/library/2PcTVc0)

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: <u>pleocytosis</u> and/or elevated <u>IgG index</u>

* <u>Oligoclonal bands</u>: helpful in diagnosing MS

* Cultures and viral <u>PCR</u>

* <u>VDRL</u> to rule out <u>syphilis</u>

* Further investigations based on clinical presentation and suspected underlying cause, e.g., paraneoplastic profile to rule out <u>paraneoplastic syndrome</u>, CT chest to rule out <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>nerve conduction studies</u> to help rule out <u>GBS</u> and peripheral neuropathies

* Differential diagnoses

* <u>Anterior spinal artery</u> <u>infarction</u>

* <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u> (<u>GBS</u>)

* <u>Compressive myelopathy</u> (e.g., due to <u>intramedullary</u> spinal cord tumors)

* Radiation <u>myelitis</u>

* Metabolic <u>myelopathy</u> (e.g., due to <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> deficiency, <u>copper deficiency</u>)

* Treatment

* Acute management

* First-line: immediate high-dose IV <u>corticosteroids</u>

* Second-line

* <u>Plasmapheresis</u> if response to <u>corticosteroids</u> is insufficient

* <u>Cyclophosphamide</u>

* <u>Supportive care</u>: prevent <u>decubitus ulcer</u> and/or <u>thrombosis</u>, manage <u>urinary retention</u>, <u>gastroparesis</u>, <u>constipation</u>, and <u>respiratory failure</u> in patients with high cervical cord lesions

* Long-term management

* Neurological <u>rehabilitation</u>

* Ongoing treatment of underlying causes (e.g., long-term immunomodulatory therapies for systemic autoimmune conditions or <u>demyelinating</u> disease)





![Transverse myelitis](media/qcctbu6n4hcjfwunsfofakjp.jpg)

Transverse myelitis




#### Other




* <u>Vasculitis</u>: resulting from <u>connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>polyarteritis nodosa</u>, <u>granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>, <u>Behcet disease</u>)

* Infections

* <u>Neuroborreliosis</u>: diagnosed by <u>CSF</u> examination (intrathecal <u>Borrelia</u>-specific <u>antibodies</u>, <u>lymphocytosis</u>)

* <u>Neurosyphilis</u>: diagnosed by a TPHA <u>screening test</u>

* <u>Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy</u> (<u>PML</u>): perform an <u>HIV test</u>

* <u>HIV</u>-<u>encephalopathy</u>: perform an <u>HIV test</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### General principles [[35]](/library/s5XtlA)




* All patients: Refer to a <u>neurologist</u> for specialized management.

* Acute exacerbations: Treat all acute exacerbations that affect physical functioning.

* First line: high-dose IV or PO <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u>)

* Alternatives: <u>plasmapheresis</u> or <u>adrenocorticotropic hormone</u> (<u>ACTH</u>) gel [[36]](/library/9OYNu6)

* Long-term management: Combine pharmacological and nonpharmacological measures to prevent exacerbations and improve quality of life.

* <u>Disease-modifying MS therapy</u>

* Lifestyle modifications (e.g., exercise, <u>smoking cessation</u>) and management of comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease, <u>sleep disorders</u>)

* <u>Vitamin D</u> supplementation may be beneficial.  [[37]](/library/yFcdkV0)

* Management of symptoms (e.g., <u>spasticity</u>, <u>central neuropathic pain</u>, <u>bowel and bladder dysfunction</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Treatment should be initiated as early as possible; the goals of treatment are to manage the primary exacerbation, prevent further exacerbations, and slow disease progression.




### Management of acute <u>MS exacerbations</u> [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[38]](/library/mFcViV0)




If an acute exacerbation of MS is suspected, a specialist should be consulted immediately for management.




* Preferred therapy: 

* High-dose <u>glucocorticoid</u> <u>pulse</u> therapy (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE)  [[38]](/library/mFcViV0)[[39]](/library/bFcHgV0)[[40]](/library/qW1Cmf0)

* Start measures to <u>prevent complications of glucocorticoid therapy</u> (e.g., <u>PPIs</u>, monitoring for <u>hyperglycemia</u>).

* Alternatives: <u>plasmapheresis</u>, <u>ACTH gel</u>  [[38]](/library/mFcViV0)[[41]](/library/5FciiV0)

* Additional considerations

* Perform a thorough <u>neurological examination</u> and compare with the patient's baseline.

* Evaluate for possible infectious triggers.  [[42]](/library/CW1qnf0)

* Consider hospital admission for patients with disabling symptoms (e.g., loss of <u>vision</u>, difficulty with ambulation, <u>dysphagia</u>). [[43]](/library/EX18-20)

* <u>Supportive care</u>: <u>physical therapy</u>, <u>occupational therapy</u>, and/or speech and swallow evaluations





> [!TIP]
> Mild exacerbations that do not impact physical functioning may not require medical treatment.




### Disease-modifying MS therapy




* There are multiple disease-modifying drugs available to treat MS.

* The decision about agent requires careful consideration of: 

* Individual patient's characteristics (e.g., clinical <u>phenotype</u>, comorbidities)

* Medication side effects

* Other factors (e.g., medication availability, route of administration)

* All patients receiving <u>disease-modifying therapy for MS</u> should use <u>birth control</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Disease-modifying therapy for MS</u> is generally not recommended for pregnant and <u>breastfeeding</u> patients. [[44]](/library/ckXa5y)




| Commonly used <u>disease-modifying MS drugs</u> by clinical <u>phenotype</u> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Phenotype</u> | Drugs commonly used |
| <br><u>Clinically isolated syndrome</u> [[45]](/library/28cTNV0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Interferon</u> therapy (IFN-β)<br><br>* <u>Glatiramer acetate</u><br><br>* <u>Teriflunomide</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Relapsing-remitting MS</u> [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Interferon</u> therapy (IFN-β)<br><br>* <u>Glatiramer acetate</u><br><br>* Fumarates (e.g., <u>dimethyl fumarate</u>)<br><br>* <u>Teriflunomide</u><br><br>* Sphingosine 1-<u>phosphate</u> <u>receptor</u> modulators (e.g., <u>fingolimod</u>, <u>siponimod</u>)<br><br>* <u>Monoclonal antibodies</u> (e.g., <u>natalizumab</u>, <u>ocrelizumab</u>, <u>alemtuzumab</u>, <u>ofatumumab</u>)<br><br>* <u>Mitoxantrone</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Secondary progressive MS</u> [[46]](/library/e8cxlV0)<br> | <br>* All disease-modifying therapies may be used for active <u>SP-MS</u>.<br><br> |
| <br><u>Primary progressive MS</u> [[47]](/library/V8cGlV0)<br> | <br>* <u>Ocrelizumab</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Monoclonal antibodies</u> (e.g., <u>natalizumab</u>, <u>ocrelizumab</u>) have the highest <u>efficacy</u> for reducing exacerbations, but lower <u>efficacy</u> medications (e.g., <u>interferon beta</u>, <u>glatiramer acetate</u>) often have fewer side effects. [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)

### <u>Supportive care</u> and symptom management [[7]](/library/DGc1YV0)[[59]](/library/VFcGSV0)[[60]](/library/kFcmRV0)




Consider any of the following measures in a management plan tailored to the individual patient:




* General measures

* Encourage physical activity.

* Close follow-up with <u>neurology</u> and primary care

* Ancillary referral as needed (e.g., physical therapists, occupational therapists, psychologists)

* Screen for major <u>depression</u> and start therapy with <u>antidepressants</u> as needed (see also “Treatment” in “Major <u>depression</u> disorder”).

* Urinary and bowel dysfunction

* <u>Urinary frequency</u>: <u>pelvic floor physical therapy</u>, <u>bladder training</u>; Consider <u>anticholinergics</u> (e.g., <u>oxybutynin</u>) and <u>antimuscarinics</u> (e.g., <u>tolterodine</u>).

* <u>Urinary retention</u>: Consider <u>intermittent catheterization</u> and <u>parasympathomimetic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>bethanechol</u>). [[61]](/library/NFc-RV0)

* Bowel dysfunction: <u>dietary fiber</u> and fluid intake; <u>laxatives</u> (e.g., <u>senna</u>) and <u>stool softeners</u> (e.g., <u>docusate</u>) as needed

* <u>Spasticity</u>

* Stretching, avoidance of triggers (e.g., certain positions, <u>pain</u>, <u>constipation</u>)

* Medications: <u>baclofen</u> (centrally acting <u>GABA</u> <u>agonist</u>), <u>tizanidine</u> (α<sub>2</sub>-<u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u>), <u>gabapentin</u>, <u>dantrolene</u>, <u>botulinum toxin</u>.

* <u>Tremors</u>: <u>deep brain stimulation</u> techniques, <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>propranolol</u>), <u>gabapentin</u>

* <u>Central neuropathic pain</u>: <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u> (e.g., <u>amitriptyline</u>): , other <u>antidepressants</u> (e.g., <u>duloxetine</u>), <u>anticonvulsants</u> (e.g., <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>gabapentin</u>), <u>transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation</u> (see also “Treatment” in “<u>Trigeminal</u> <u>Neuralgia</u>”)

* Walking difficulties: mobility aids (e.g., canes, walkers), consider dalfampridine  [[62]](/library/2U1TcT0)

* Others

* Fatigue: Consider medications such as <u>amantadine</u> or <u>modafinil</u>.

* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u>: Consider medications for <u>erectile dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>sildenafil</u>) and nonpharmacological measures (e.g., vaginal lubricants, <u>intracavernous injection therapy</u>) as needed.

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: to reduce potential psychological issues (e.g., <u>depression</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Physical therapy</u>, <u>occupational therapy</u>, and <u>psychotherapy</u> are safe, nonpharmacological options that can improve multiple symptoms in patients with MS, including <u>spasticity</u>, fatigue, walking difficulties, and <u>central neuropathic pain</u>.

---

## Prognosis

### Poor prognostic factors for disease progression [[63]](/library/t5XXNA)[[64]](/library/G5XBlA)




* Male sex

* Age at MS onset > 40 years

* Multiple symptoms with early motor and <u>cerebellar</u> involvement

* Incomplete recovery after exacerbations

* High relapse rate in the first 2 years after MS onset
